notes.2a: This was usually well answered but some Co 3+ ions were described with 3d electrons present.
notes.2b: (i) Many answers described the ligands as ‘surrounding’ the metal ion. While this is true it does not distinguish between a complex ion and, for example, a solvated sodium ion. The answer needed to include a simple description of bonding between the ligands and the metal ion.
notes.2bii: Some answers incorrectly suggested physical properties, such as high melting point.
notes.2c: Candidates should have been able to apply their knowledge of transition metal reactions here.
notes.2d: (ii) Many candidates correctly worked out that the three copper species had a total oxidation number of +7 and the consequent average oxidation number.
notes.2diii: Candidates found this question difficult, even when they had received credit for their answer to (ii).
notes.3a: (i) This diagram was drawn well with many candidates receiving credit.
notes.3aii: Candidates made good use of the Data Booklet in answering this question.
notes.3b: Most candidates gave the correct answer here.
notes.3c: A few candidates gave well-argued answers, explaining the effect of lower Cl – concentration on the electrode potential of the Cl 2/Cl - half cell, and therefore on the overall cell potential. Some answers referred to the ‘electrode potential of Cl – /Cl 2’ rather than the usual reduction potential; this often generated a confused answer.
notes.3d: (i) The incorrect half equations seen included the use of acid conditions, and half equations with H2 or O2 as products rather than reactants.
notes.3dii: Candidates struggled to answer here if their equations in (i) were not correct.
notes.3iii: Answers needed to refer to the specific reasons for the advantage rather than the vague ‘environmentally friendly’ or ‘cheaper’. Specific and correct answers that referred to the ease and speed of recharging, or the non-toxicity of the water product, were comparatively rare.
notes.4a: (i) Most candidates were confident in answering this question.
notes.4b: (i) This was generally answered well, although some stated that amphoteric substances are both acidic and alkaline, rather than both acidic and basic.
notes.4bii: The equation was constructed correctly by approximately half of all candidates.
notes.4c: (i) The correct information was usually quoted, although some gave the E o for the reduction of Sn 2+ to 2+ 4+ Sn, rather than the oxidation of Sn to Sn .
notes.4cii: Many candidates were awarded full credit for this question.
notes.4d: (i) This was generally answered well. Some answers described ‘oxidation and reduction happening at the same time’, rather than ‘oxidation and reduction of the same species/of germanium/of GeO’.
notes.4dii: This completely novel context was found difficult by many. Candidates should be encouraged to use the blank spaces on question papers to write any useful working. In this case it was hoped that candidates would write the equation for the reaction of chlorine with cold aqueous sodium hydroxide. This could then have been used to work out the answer to the question. This approach was very rare.
notes.4iii: Approximately half of all candidates gained credit for their diagram. Most of the incorrect diagrams had either a double or triple bond between the carbon atoms, or had no lone pair on one or both of the nitrogen atoms.
notes.4e: (i) The information ‘All the phosphorus atoms in P4 are trivalent’ was often ignored.
notes.4eii: Most candidates understood the principle of endothermic bond breaking and exothermic bond making and were able to use their answer to (i) to gain at least partial credit.
notes.4f: (i) Candidates made good attempts at this equation.
notes.4fii: The instructions in the question were often not used to suggest the structure.
notes.5a: (i) L and M were better answered than N.
notes.5iii: Candidates who described N correctly in (i) generally gained credit here.
notes.5iv: The correct answer, oxidation, was very rarely seen. Some candidates answered ‘substitution, oxidation and cleavage’. If an approach like this is taken it must be all correct, in this reaction the first steps are addition and elimination rather than substitution.
notes.5b: (i) Candidates should be encouraged to use the question paper as it was intended. In this case the box was labelled ‘intermediate’ with the reagents on the left of it and products on the right. However, many answers were seen with the complete mechanism described in the intermediate box. Full credit was available for this approach, providing all necessary information was included.
notes.5bii: Candidates found it difficult to apply the information given in the question here.

notes.6bii: The low temperature needed for the formation of the diazonium ion was better known than the use of NaNO2/HCl in step 1. The use of alkaline conditions was not well known in step 2.

notes.8iii: Part (b) of this question told candidates twice that Y is an ester, but a significant number did not use this information.

notes.9c: (i) The instruction to label a bond was missed by some candidates who may have been looking for answer lines such as were found elsewhere. Some candidates indicated an atom rather than a bond; others used a circle rather than an arrow. If such a circle included the correct bond and part of an incorrect bond no credit was given. However this question was generally well answered.
notes.9d: Some incorrect answers did not identify the relevant features of molecule W as instructed in the question. Other incorrect answers referred to –OH groups, these are not present in molecule W.
notes.key_messages:
The question paper requires answers to be written in dark blue or black ink, the use of pencils by candidates
in writing formulae, structures and equations is to be strongly discouraged. Pencilled text is sometimes too
faint to read and also some candidates write over the pencil in ink so that their answers become illegible.
notes.general_comments:
Candidates should be encouraged to use blank spaces on the question paper for their own working to aid
them in answering questions.
